gaps.sentence: You really ___ to apologise before this gets worse.
gaps.explanation: 'Ought to' expresses advice similar to 'should': ought to apologise.

gaps.sentence: The theatre was completely empty, so the performance ___ have been very popular.
gaps.explanation: 'Can't have' draws a negative conclusion from evidence: can't have been.

gaps.sentence: She ___ have lied to the police — it was a serious mistake.
gaps.explanation: 'Shouldn't have' plus the participle criticizes a past action: shouldn't have.

gaps.sentence: That ___ be Sarah at the door — she is in Berlin until Friday.
gaps.explanation: 'Can't' expresses logical impossibility: can't be Sarah.

gaps.sentence: ___ you swim when you were four years old?
gaps.explanation: 'Could' asks about past ability: Could you swim.

gaps.sentence: You ___ bring your own laptop — we will provide everything.
gaps.hint: no obligation, so needn't not mustn't
gaps.explanation: 'Needn't' means it is not necessary; 'mustn't' would mean it is prohibited: needn't bring.

gaps.sentence: When I was a child, I ___ stay up late on New Year's Eve.
gaps.hint: permission that existed in the past
gaps.explanation: 'Was allowed to' expresses past permission; 'could' is also possible: was allowed to.

gaps.sentence: You ___ be starving — you haven't eaten since breakfast.
gaps.explanation: 'Must' expresses a logical deduction about the present.
